questions.questionText: Given two branches that have diverged from a common ancestor, how does the operational mechanism of a 3-way merge differ from a fast-forward merge in terms of the resulting repository state?
options: A 3-way merge creates a new synthetic commit with two parents, whereas a fast-forward merge simply moves the branch pointer linearly to the target commit.
A 3-way merge deletes the common ancestor commit to save space, whereas a fast-forward merge retains the full history including the common ancestor commit.
A 3-way merge moves the branch pointer linearly to the latest commit, whereas a fast-forward merge creates a new synthetic commit with two parents.
A 3-way merge requires manual resolution of all conflicts before any pointer movement, whereas a fast-forward merge automatically resolves conflicts by discarding local changes.
questions.correctAnswer: A 3-way merge creates a new synthetic commit with two parents, whereas a fast-forward merge simply moves the branch pointer linearly to the target commit.
questions.explanation: The evidence states that a fast-forward merge moves the branch pointer forward linearly when no divergence exists, while a 3-way merge creates a synthetic merge commit with two parents when divergent histories exist. The correct option accurately contrasts these two distinct operational outcomes: pointer movement versus new commit creation. The second option inverts these mechanisms (Misconception Inversion). The third option introduces untaught behavior regarding automatic conflict resolution and discarding changes (Scope Precondition Error). The fourth option invents a mechanism of deleting ancestors which is not supported by the evidence (Distinct Alternative/Invention).
